title: Split binding controller and orphaned allocation reclaim into smaller services
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary: The current GPU fleet controller runs a monolithic binding + reclaim loop that handles node allocation, GPU binding, lease heartbeats, and orphaned allocation reclamation. This ticket refactors that monolith into two clearer responsibilities: (1) a lightweight Binding Controller responsible for fast, idempotent node->allocation assignment and node state transitions, and (2) an Orphaned Allocation Reclaimer service that runs less frequently, performs expensive scans, and handles repair workflows.

Motivation: Over the past year we've seen multiple incidents where a slow scan path (or a lock contention spike during reclaim) causes binding latency to spike and SLOs to degrade for tail latency. Separating responsibilities should give us: 
- Lower p99 binding latency under noisy reclaim workloads
- Simplified reasoning about lease life and state transitions
- Smaller blast radius for future autoscaler changes and capacity-planner tuning

Goals (measured):
- Reduce binding loop p99 from ~720ms to <250ms under reclaim load (load test baseline: 1K concurrent allocations).
- Reduce CPU contention on fleet-controller nodes by 40% during reclaim windows in canary clusters.
- Provide clear metrics and alerts for stale/orphaned allocation growth and reclaim throughput.

Scope:
- Implement the Binding Controller (always-on, event-driven): handles node binding, lease refresh, and fast reconciliation. Must be idempotent and safe to run in multiple replicas.
- Implement the Orphaned Allocation Reclaimer (cron/worker): periodic scan, multi-step reclaim (mark-stale -> attempt-repair -> force-reclaim), and controlled backoff.
- Migrate existing code paths from the monolith and add feature flags for gradual rollout.

Out of scope:
- Autoscaler policy redesign (handled in separate tickets).
- Persistent storage schema changes beyond lightweight indices for reclaim scans.

Design decisions and trade-offs:
- Use optimistic concurrency for binding (compare-and-swap on allocation record) to avoid coarse locking. This means occasional binding conflicts but much lower contention.
- Reclaimer will use paged scans with a cursor stored in Redis to avoid large table full scans; this intentionally trades eventual reclaim speed for stable CPU usage.
- Keep the existing lease TTL semantics; we will not shorten TTLs in this refactor to avoid ripples into other systems.

Implementation plan (phases):
1) Spike (1 week): benchmark current binding + reclaim under synthetic noise. Implement micro-prototypes for optimistic binding and paged scan. Collect perf numbers.
2) Binding Controller (2 sprints): implement, unit tests, e2e tests, feature-flag behind FF_BINDING_V2. Canary in dev cluster.
3) Reclaimer (2 sprints): implement paged scan with cursor, repair flow, metrics, FF_RECLAIM_V2.
4) Migrate (1 sprint): flip feature flag in canary, monitor for 2 weeks, progressively roll to prod.

Rollout and safety:
- All changes behind feature flags with kill switch.
- Start with 1 canary cluster (us-west-2-dev), then 3 internal clusters, then prod.
- Add conservative circuit-breaker: if binding latency p99 increases by >25% in 10m, auto-disable the new binding controller.

Monitoring and alerts:
- New metrics: binding_controller_latency_seconds_bucket, reclaim_scan_cursor_age_seconds, orphaned_allocation_count, reclaim_throughput_per_minute.
- Alert: orphaned_allocation_count > 1000 for 15m -> Severity P1.
- Dashboards: quick view for binding latency and reclaim progress with links to canary logs.

Migration notes:
- Existing in-flight allocations: Binding Controller must honor allocations with active leases. Reclaimer will only operate on allocations with lease expired > reclaim_grace_seconds.
- Database indices: add a composite index on (state, last_update) to support paged scans; apply in a maintenance window.

Open questions:
- Should the Reclaimer have a soft-rate limit per cluster to avoid starving repair attempts in very large fleets? (proposal: yes, start with 100 reparations / minute per region).
- How to surface partial progress to ops dashboard during a reclaim sweep? (proposal: show scanning cursor and recent repaired IDs).

Acceptance criteria:
- All unit and integration tests passing.
- Binding controller reduces p99 binding latency by target in canary tests.
- Reclaimer demonstrates stable CPU usage and completes sweep of 100k allocations in <8 hours in test environment.
- Feature flags able to be toggled safely with documented rollback steps.

Artifacts and references:
- Design doc (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Split+Binding+and+Reclaim+Design
- Load test harness and results: https://internal.redwood.ai/dashboards/gpu-fleet/bench/2025-01-binding-reclaim-spike
- Prototype PRs: https://github.com/redwood-inference/gpu-fleet/pull/482, https://github.com/redwood-inference/gpu-fleet/pull/509

Next tasks:
- Spike results review with runtime team (scheduled 2025-01-16).
- Create skeleton repos and API contracts for the two controllers.
- Schedule DB maintenance window for index creation.
